copy.hero_line_5: READ EACH WELL ON ITS OWN
copy.home_intro: A royalty check is the end of several calculations, not the beginning. Work backward from the deposited amount to barrels sold, realized price, deductions, taxes, decimal interest, and each well's age. That sequence turns a changing check into a production story that can be compared with a cash offer.
copy.home_basins: Bakken, Permian, Eagle Ford, DJ, Delaware, Midland, and Powder River wells do not share one universal decline profile. Depth, lateral length, stacked benches, weather, gathering, regulation, and operator sequencing all change the line. Basin pages explain the local variables before an owner compares timing.

about_blocks: THE CHECK IS A RESULT, NOT AN EXPLANATION

A deposited royalty amount blends production volume, product mix, realized price, deductions, taxes, decimal interest, timing, and sometimes several wells at different ages. The first task is to separate those inputs. Once the lease total is split well by well and month by month, normal decline becomes easier to distinguish from a pricing change, shut-in, new completion, or statement error.
DEFINE THE TERM BEFORE USING IT

Hyperbolic decline, netback, held by production, division order, allocation, and title curative are useful only when their effect is plain. Every review starts with a short definition and then connects the term to an actual line on a statement, deed, lease, or public well record. The technical label should make the decision clearer, never hide it.
BUILD THE CURVE FROM REAL MONTHS

Peak production is not a lifetime average. A horizontal oil well usually falls fastest early and then enters a longer, slower tail. Plotting actual months exposes that transition. Weather, curtailment, workovers, downtime, new wells, and stacked development are then marked separately so temporary events are not mistaken for the underlying curve.
KEEP VALUE AND TITLE IN THE SAME FILE

A strong production forecast cannot close a transaction if ownership is unclear. Deeds, probate, trusts, marital interests, prior reservations, assignments, and the paid decimal belong beside the economic review from the start. That parallel track reduces late surprises and makes any accepted offer easier to compare with the interest that can actually be conveyed.
END WITH A DECISION, NOT A SALES SCRIPT

The useful outcomes are specific: hold the interest, sell a defined portion, sell the full interest, gather one missing record, or wait for a known event. No single answer fits every owner or every well. A good review makes the remaining uncertainty visible and gives the owner enough structure to compare the next check with the present cash option.

investing: {name} should begin with actual net deposits, not a headline about passive income. Gather at least twelve months of statements when available and split the total by well, product, volume, realized price, deductions, taxes, and decimal interest. A new horizontal well can produce a large early check and then decline sharply; a mature conventional well may be smaller but steadier. Those are different income shapes even when the latest deposit is identical. Plot the months before applying a multiple. Then mark downtime, new completions, workovers, and price changes so one unusual period does not distort the base case. This first pass answers whether the income is concentrated in one young well, diversified across several tails, or dependent on an event that may not repeat.
Separate the curve from the commodity

Production decline and oil price movement are separate risks. Volume can fall while the check rises because price improved, or volume can hold while the check falls because realized price weakened or deductions increased. For {name}, build at least three views: a production-only curve, a price-and-netback view, and a combined cash-flow view. The production view shows reservoir and operating behavior. The netback view shows what remains after transportation, gathering, processing, taxes, and other allowed charges. The combined view shows what actually reaches the owner. Keeping the three views separate prevents a temporary price rally from being mistaken for improved well performance and prevents a weak price month from being mistaken for a mechanical problem.

A mineral package can contain producing royalty, undeveloped minerals, multiple operators, several formations, and tracts spread across more than one county. {name} needs each source identified before risk is summarized. Producing royalty is modeled from existing well history. Undeveloped value depends more on permits, nearby completions, operator inventory, spacing, and the chance that a future well reaches the tract. Concentration matters at every level: one operator, one pad, one commodity, one county, or one early-life well can dominate the result. A clear review states which part of the value is supported by current checks and which part depends on development that has not occurred.
Turn the review into a decision rule

The last step for {name} is not a prediction stated as certainty. It is a decision rule. Define the amount of near-term cash needed, the income an owner is willing to keep exposed to decline and price, the portion of undeveloped upside worth retaining, and the records still missing. Compare a hold case, partial-sale case, and full-sale case on the same assumptions. Note what would change the choice: a new permit, a division-order correction, a title issue, a price threshold, or another year of production history. That structure makes the tradeoff visible without pretending the future path of oil prices or operator activity is known.
exchange-1031: Put the exchange question before the sale

{name} begins before sale proceeds are received. A seller considering tax deferral should speak with a qualified intermediary and independent tax counsel before closing or taking control of funds. The working file should identify the relinquished interest, expected closing date, sale structure, taxpayer name, and the property rights actually being conveyed. Mineral and royalty interests can raise state-specific and fact-specific questions, so general examples are not a substitute for advice on the transaction. Starting early preserves options; waiting until proceeds are already controlled can remove them.

The exchange file for {name} should show the identification deadline and completion deadline as calendar dates, not only as rules. The 45-day window is used to identify replacement property in writing under the chosen identification rule. The 180-day window is used to complete the acquisition, subject to the applicable tax-return deadline. These periods run concurrently, so the second clock does not start after the first ends. Add qualified-intermediary instructions, lender milestones, title review, inspections, due diligence, and backup choices to the same calendar.
Match the taxpayer and the property rights

A 1031 exchange depends on continuity that can be lost when names, entities, or ownership rights change without planning. For {name}, compare the taxpayer on the relinquished property with the taxpayer expected to acquire the replacement. Confirm how the mineral or royalty interest is classified under the relevant law and how title is held. Trusts, estates, partnerships, disregarded entities, marital ownership, and recent transfers deserve early professional review. The practical goal is simple: do not let a preventable ownership mismatch appear after the identification window has closed.
Keep primary and backup property evidence together

{name} needs more than a list of possible replacements. For each candidate, record the property description, asking price or value evidence, debt assumptions, expected income, management demands, title status, inspection access, seller cooperation, and closing risk. Rank primary and backup choices before identification. If a partial exchange or taxable boot is possible, show that scenario separately. The exchange decision should remain tied to the seller's goals and independent advice, not to pressure created by a narrowing deadline.
Close with a complete exchange record

The final file for {name} should preserve the sale agreement, settlement statement, assignment to the qualified intermediary, written identification, delivery evidence, replacement-property contract, title documents, loan records, acquisition settlement statement, and professional advice used for the return. Reconcile dates and dollar amounts before the file is archived. If some proceeds were retained, debt was not fully replaced, or more than one replacement was acquired, flag those facts for the tax professional instead of assuming the result. A complete record cannot guarantee tax treatment, but it gives the owner and advisers a clear trail from relinquished interest through replacement closing.
